query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A post-solidification, low‐temperature aging heat treatment that induces a uniform dispersion of nanoscale precipitates along the internal lamellar boundaries will simultaneously enhance strength and improve tensile ductility in eutectic high‐entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventionally processed eutectic high‐entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies that exhibit numerous internal boundaries and a brittle room-temperature tensile response.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, low‐temperature aging treatment after solution treatment to cause homogeneous nanoscale precipitation along the lamellar colony boundaries.
generation.conditions: After solution treating the as‐cast alloy, perform aging at approximately 450–500 °C for several hours (e.g., 4–8 hours) in an inert (argon) atmosphere; subsequently, subject samples to room-temperature tensile testing at a standard strain rate (e.g., ~10−3 s−1) to evaluate mechanical properties.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of well‐dispersed nanoscale precipitates along the lamellar interfaces
generation.mechanism: The nanoscale precipitates are expected to improve load transfer between phases and blunt microcrack initiation/propagation by reinforcing the interlamellar regions. This dual role obstructs dislocation motion to raise strength while simultaneously toughening critical boundaries to improve ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated lamellar microstructure, the aging treatment is predicted to increase both the ultimate tensile strength and the room-temperature tensile ductility.
generation.baseline: Eutectic high‐entropy alloy processed by conventional methods resulting in brittle lamellar colonies with low tensile ductility.
generation.boundary: This intervention is applicable provided that the precipitates remain nanoscale and uniformly distributed; excessive coarsening or overaging may instead degrade ductility. The approach is expected to be effective primarily for eutectic alloys with similar dual-phase lamellar morphologies.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal aging temperature and time, as well as the precise precipitate chemistry and distribution needed for balancing strength and ductility, remain to be determined through systematic studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one using the conventional processing route and the other undergoing the additional aging treatment. Characterize the microstructure (using SEM/TEM to confirm the presence of nanoscale precipitates along lamellar boundaries) and perform standardized room-temperature tensile tests to obtain stress-strain curves.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aging-treated samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in both UTS and ductility compared to the conventionally processed baseline, or if precipitate coarsening is observed that correlates with no or negative improvements, the hypothesis will be falsified.
